worked.title: Revisit rows without duplicating them
worked.explanation: The first case updates an existing amount and adds a late record within the allowed window. It then reruns the model to verify the same three identified values. This checks the combination of selection and write semantics.
worked.expected: Final amounts are id 1=6, id 2=7 and id 3=9, with three rows after rerun.

worked.title: Expose the limit of a finite lookback
worked.explanation: The second case adds a record older than the ten-unit window. A normal update misses it, while full refresh recovers it. The result makes the lateness assumption visible rather than describing lookback as universal correctness.
worked.expected: Normal output has 1 row; a declared full refresh produces 2.

exercises.title: Test the exact boundary
exercises.task: Add a record at max(updated_at)-10.
exercises.check: The inclusive predicate considers it.
exercises.hint: The operator is >=.
exercises.answer: Record whether the business policy includes that boundary and test it explicitly. A small operator change can alter historical coverage.

exercises.title: Repeat a correction
exercises.task: Apply the same corrected source twice.
exercises.check: The identified result remains unchanged.
exercises.hint: Check both values and row count.
exercises.answer: Idempotency requires deterministic selection and matching. Comparing only a total can miss offsetting duplicate and missing records.

exercises.title: Duplicate a source key
exercises.task: Add two selected records with one id.
exercises.check: A separate key test detects the ambiguity.
exercises.hint: unique_key is not an automatic source uniqueness guarantee.
exercises.answer: Resolve versions before the incremental write or fail the build. Arbitrary ordering can otherwise determine which state survives.

exercises.title: Widen the lookback
exercises.task: Include a previously missed old record by changing the window.
exercises.check: The record is selected under the revised policy.
exercises.hint: Measure added work as well as correctness.
exercises.answer: A wider window changes compute and still has a limit. Choose it from observed/contracted lateness and maintain a separate repair process.

exercises.title: Compare with full recomputation
exercises.task: Rebuild the small fixture and compare keyed rows.
exercises.check: The accepted incremental case matches.
exercises.hint: Use stable ordering and schema.
exercises.answer: This is a strong regression for the fixture. Production completeness still depends on the source versioning and arrival contract.

exercises.title: Specify a correction ledger
exercises.task: List what should be recorded for a backfill.
exercises.check: It includes identity, time scope, source version and reconciliation.
exercises.hint: A repair needs reproducible evidence.
exercises.answer: Retain the reason, affected keys or partitions, input version, old/new checks and publication decision. Do not silently rewrite historical outputs.

units.diagnosis: If a keyed update creates duplicates, inspect selected-source uniqueness rather than assuming unique_key enforced it. If old corrections are missed, inspect the lookback bound. If a rerun changes results without source changes, inspect ordering, nondeterministic expressions and external state.
units.transfer: Explain which late arrivals it accepts, which require repair and how the result is reconciled with a full recomputation. Keep the policy explicit as data volume grows.
units.lab: Apply a delete+insert model with a ten-unit lookback to a correction and a late insert, rerun it without duplicates, and show that a record outside the window needs a full refresh.
references: dbt docs: About microbatch incremental models

units.title: Snapshots and observed historical state
units.outcome: Explain what a snapshot actually observed and what it cannot reconstruct.
key_terms: Snapshot
A dbt resource that records a mutable source's state each time it runs, adding a version row when a tracked row has changed.
Type 2 slowly changing dimension
A history table that keeps one row per observed version of an entity, each with its own validity interval.
check strategy
A snapshot strategy that detects a change by comparing the listed `check_cols` with the current version.
dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to
The columns bounding when a row was the observed version; dbt_valid_to is null for the current version.
hard_deletes
The snapshot setting for rows that vanish from the source; `invalidate` closes the current version by setting its dbt_valid_to.
units.theory:
A snapshot records changes in a mutable source as observed by successive snapshot runs. It can support slowly changing dimension history, but it cannot recover states that were never observed between runs. Its validity intervals describe the snapshot's chosen strategy and clock. Those intervals should not automatically be treated as the true business-effective time of every change.

The example uses the check strategy to detect a change in region for a stable customer identifier. dbt stores a closed historical version and a current version. The second case also removes a customer from the source and uses hard_deletes='invalidate' so the previously current record is closed. Without a declared deletion policy, consumers can misinterpret missing source records.

History is meaningful only with a stable identity and clear column choices. A changed display name, a corrected attribute and a genuinely new entity are different events. Decide which changes create new versions and which time interpretation the downstream consumer requires.
units.syntax: The modern YAML snapshot declares a relation, unique_key, strategy, check_cols and deletion policy. The example obtains the actual relation name from the generated manifest because custom schema naming can depend on the adapter/profile. dbt_valid_to is null for current versions under this contract. Query both all historical rows and the active subset.

worked.title: Observe an attribute change
worked.explanation: The first case snapshots two customers, changes one region, and snapshots again. The history has three versions in total, with two current customers. The old region remains observable rather than being overwritten.
worked.expected: There are 3 history rows; current regions are west and south.

worked.title: Invalidate a deleted source entity
worked.explanation: The second case changes one customer and removes the other. The explicit deletion policy closes the removed customer's current version. It does not invent a new active customer or silently erase history.
worked.expected: History still has 3 rows, but only customer 1/west is current.

exercises.title: Inspect a closed version
exercises.task: Query the old region and its validity endpoint.

reasoning.why: The check strategy compared region for customer 1, saw north change to west and closed the north row by setting dbt_valid_to. That is why the snapshot holds 3 rows for 2 customers after the second run.
reasoning.wrong: Querying only where dbt_valid_to is null returns west for customer 1 and loses the north interval, which answers what is current rather than what was observed before.
reasoning.verify: Select customer_id, region, dbt_valid_from, dbt_valid_to from the relation named in the manifest where customer_id = 1; expect north with a non-null dbt_valid_to and west with null.

exercises.check: The changed version has a non-null dbt_valid_to.
exercises.hint: Current and historical predicates differ.
exercises.answer: Retain both versions and their interval meaning. A current-only query is appropriate for a different question than a historical reconstruction.

exercises.title: Change a tracked column
exercises.task: Add another attribute to check_cols.

reasoning.why: check_cols lists the columns whose change opens a new version. Adding segment means a later seed that edits only segment closes the current row, which is right if segment is business state and wasteful if it is load metadata.
reasoning.wrong: Switching check_cols to all would also version on columns like a load batch id that change every run, producing a new history row per customer per snapshot without any real change.
reasoning.verify: Add segment to the seed and check_cols, snapshot, change only segment for customer 2 and snapshot again; the history count should grow by one row for customer 2.

exercises.check: Its changes can create new versions under the revised policy.
exercises.hint: The tracked column set is part of the contract.
exercises.answer: Review whether the attribute represents meaningful state or noisy metadata. Tracking every field can produce unnecessary history churn.

exercises.title: Explain unobserved changes
exercises.task: Describe a source that changes twice between snapshot runs.

reasoning.why: A snapshot only compares the source at each invocation. If region goes north to east to west between two runs, the stored history shows north then west, and east never existed as far as the table can tell.
reasoning.wrong: Shortening dbt_valid_from intervals or interpolating an east row from the gap would invent state that no run observed.
reasoning.verify: Write east to the seed without running snapshot, then write west and snapshot; querying customer 1 returns exactly two rows, north and west, with no east.

exercises.check: The intermediate state may never appear in the snapshot.
exercises.hint: Observation frequency limits evidence.
exercises.answer: Use a source change log or another stronger history mechanism when the intermediate state matters. Snapshots cannot reconstruct unobserved facts.

exercises.title: Compare deletion policies
exercises.task: Explain the effect of ignoring source deletions.

reasoning.why: In example_two customer 2 disappears and hard_deletes invalidate closes its row, leaving only customer 1 active. With ignore, the south row for customer 2 would remain open as if still current.
reasoning.wrong: Choosing invalidate on a feed that sometimes lands partially would close valid customers whenever a load is truncated, so a partial file looks like mass churn.
reasoning.verify: Rerun example_two with hard_deletes set to ignore; the active query should return both (1, west) and (2, south), whereas invalidate returns only (1, west).

exercises.check: A formerly current record can remain open.
exercises.hint: Missing source data needs interpretation.
exercises.answer: Choose a policy that distinguishes genuine deletion from incomplete ingestion. A partial load should not automatically invalidate valid entities.

exercises.title: Review temporal meaning
exercises.task: Distinguish snapshot observation time from business-effective time.

reasoning.why: dbt_valid_from is the time the snapshot run saw the change, not when the customer moved. A move on Monday captured by a Thursday run is recorded as Thursday.
reasoning.wrong: Joining orders to region by dbt_valid_from as if it were the effective date assigns Monday through Wednesday orders to the old region.
reasoning.verify: Add an effective_date column to the seed with a date earlier than the run, snapshot, and compare it to dbt_valid_from; the two differ, which shows they come from different clocks.

exercises.check: The explanation keeps the clocks separate.
exercises.hint: The check strategy observes changes when it runs.
exercises.answer: For event-effective analyses, preserve source effective/known times and define a temporal model. Do not infer them from snapshot timing alone.

exercises.title: Verify identity
exercises.task: Add a source uniqueness test on customer_id.

reasoning.why: unique_key customer_id assumes one source row per customer. If the seed holds two rows for customer 1 with different regions, the snapshot cannot tell which one is the observed state.
reasoning.wrong: Deduplicating with select distinct still leaves two rows when the regions differ, so the ambiguity passes through to history.
reasoning.verify: Add a unique data test on customers.customer_id, seed a duplicate id, and run dbt test; the test should fail before any snapshot run is trusted.

exercises.check: Conflicting identity is detected before trusting history.
exercises.hint: A stable key is required.
exercises.answer: Multiple source rows for one snapshot key need a deterministic, justified resolution or a failure. Otherwise the historical record becomes ambiguous.

units.diagnosis: Unexpected history growth may come from unstable keys or noisy tracked columns. Unexpected open records may come from the deletion policy. A historical result can also be temporally wrong even when its interval columns are well-formed. Inspect source completeness and time semantics before changing snapshot configuration.
units.transfer: Verify current and closed versions, define deletion handling, and preserve identity and clock contracts before using the history for features or analysis.
units.lab: Snapshot a customer seed with the check strategy and hard_deletes set to invalidate, change one region, and compare history rows with current rows after a deletion.
references: dbt docs: Add snapshots to your DAG

units.title: Enforced model schemas and constraint boundaries
units.outcome: Define a model schema contract and verify both accepted and rejected changes.
key_terms: Model contract
A declared list of column names and data types that a model's output must match.
contract.enforced
The setting that makes dbt compare the model's columns and types with its contract before materializing and fail on a mismatch.
Constraint
A rule such as not_null that dbt passes to the database in the table definition; whether it is enforced depends on the platform.
Explicit cast
A CAST in the model SQL that produces the declared type exactly rather than relying on the type the database infers.
units.theory:
A model contract declares the output columns and types expected by consumers. Enforcing that contract can reject an incompatible model before a replacement relation is published. It complements data tests, which inspect conditions on resulting records. Schema compatibility and data quality remain different dimensions of a reliable product.

The first model declares an integer identifier and a bigint amount. Explicit SQL casts make the intended types predictable. The second case first builds a valid table, then changes amount into incompatible text. The command must fail, and the program checks that the previously valid relation remains available for this specific failure path.

That observation is deliberately narrow. It does not establish that an entire multi-model build is atomic or that every failure rolls back every prior change. Another model may have materialized earlier, and data tests can fail after materialization. Publication needs its own project-level decision and recovery contract.
units.syntax: The model config contains contract.enforced=true and a complete column/type declaration. Column constraints such as not_null depend on database support. An explicit cast documents the intended SQL type; it should not be used to hide a value-domain error. Query actual database contents after failure to establish what state survived.

worked.title: Create a compatible relation
worked.explanation: The valid model declares two fields and produces a matching row. The program checks actual values after build. The schema is a promise to a consumer, while the row assertion is evidence about this particular fixture.
worked.expected: The model returns id 1 and amount 42 under the declared types.

worked.title: Reject incompatible output
worked.explanation: The second case changes the amount expression to varchar. Contract validation rejects the altered output, and the previous amount 42 remains in the relation. The guide treats that result as a tested failure path rather than a universal transaction guarantee.
worked.expected: The incompatible run fails and the previous valid amount remains 42.

exercises.title: Remove a declared column
exercises.task: Delete amount from the model output.

reasoning.why: contract.enforced compares the model's actual columns to the declared id and amount list before building. Dropping amount makes the actual list shorter than the declared one, so dbt refuses the run.
reasoning.wrong: Deleting the amount entry from the YAML at the same time makes the build pass, but it silently removes a field that downstream readers of contracted still select.
reasoning.verify: Change the SQL to select 1::integer as id and run dbt run --select contracted; expect a contract mismatch error naming amount, with the earlier table still holding (1, 42).

exercises.check: The enforced contract rejects the mismatch.
exercises.hint: The declared schema is complete.
exercises.answer: A consumer cannot safely assume the missing field exists. Treat removal as a compatibility change rather than silently updating the contract.

exercises.title: Add a new output field
exercises.task: Add an undeclared field and inspect enforcement.

reasoning.why: An extra currency column is also a mismatch under an enforced contract, because the declared column list is the full interface, not a minimum.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming extra columns are always safe ignores consumers that read by position or write the relation into a fixed schema, which then break or misalign.
reasoning.verify: Add 'usd'::varchar as currency to the SQL without declaring it and run; expect a contract error naming currency, then declare it with data_type varchar and confirm the build passes.

exercises.check: The schema change is explicit.
exercises.hint: More columns can still change a contract.
exercises.answer: Review the consumer interface and update/version the contract deliberately. Do not assume additional fields are harmless in every downstream system.

exercises.title: Test a null identifier
exercises.task: Return null for the constrained identifier.

reasoning.why: example_one declares a not_null constraint on id. DuckDB supports not null in its table DDL, so returning null for id should fail when dbt creates the table with that constraint.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming every adapter enforces the same constraints is wrong; some warehouses accept primary key or foreign key declarations as metadata only.
reasoning.verify: Change the SQL to select null::integer as id, 42::bigint as amount and run dbt build; expect a constraint violation, and query contracted to confirm whether the prior row survived.

exercises.check: The database/contract path reports the violation when supported.
exercises.hint: Schema type and value presence differ.
exercises.answer: Keep data tests as appropriate and inspect adapter constraint support. A declared constraint should not be advertised as enforced without actual evidence.

exercises.title: Distinguish failure stages
exercises.task: Compare the incompatible-schema case with the earlier uniqueness-test failure.

reasoning.why: In example_two the varchar amount is rejected before the table is replaced, so the earlier row (1, 42) is still readable. A unique test failure, by contrast, runs after the model is built.
reasoning.wrong: Treating both failures as equally safe misses that the data-test failure leaves new rows materialized for anyone who reads the table directly.
reasoning.verify: After the failed run, query select amount from contracted and expect 42; repeat with a duplicate id plus a unique test and observe that the new rows exist despite the test failure.

exercises.check: The two cases leave different observed state.
exercises.hint: Where validation occurs matters.
exercises.answer: A schema preflight may reject replacement earlier, while a data test can fail after materialization. Design publication around the actual sequence.

exercises.title: Check consumer assumptions
exercises.task: List properties beyond column types.

reasoning.why: The contract checks names and types only. amount as bigint says nothing about whether it is cents or dollars, gross or net, or whether a null means zero.
reasoning.wrong: Treating a passing enforced contract as proof that amount is correct confuses type compatibility with meaning.
reasoning.verify: Write the column description with grain, unit, period and null policy, then add an accepted_range or custom test that a deliberately negative amount fails.

exercises.check: They include grain, units, time and missingness.
exercises.hint: An integer field can still mean the wrong thing.
exercises.answer: Add semantic contracts and tests. Schema enforcement does not establish that amount uses the expected currency or period.

exercises.title: Plan an incompatible change
exercises.task: Describe a safe way to replace gross amount with net amount.

reasoning.why: Changing what amount means while keeping its name and bigint type passes the contract unchanged, so the contract alone cannot protect consumers from a meaning change.
reasoning.wrong: Editing the existing model in place to compute net amount ships a semantic break that every reader receives at once with no rollback point.
reasoning.verify: Create a second version with net_amount, run both side by side, compare totals per id, migrate readers, and confirm the old version still builds until it is retired.

exercises.check: It uses an explicit version and consumer migration.
exercises.hint: A type-preserving semantic change can still break users.
exercises.answer: Publish a new version with its definition, compare results, migrate consumers and retain rollback evidence. The next lesson makes version selection explicit.

units.diagnosis: A contract error may be the correct protection against an incompatible model. Inspect declared and actual column names/types instead of disabling enforcement. After failure, inspect the database and invocation artifacts; do not assume every relation reverted to a prior state.
units.transfer: Keep the observed failure timing separate from broader transaction claims, and combine structural compatibility with semantic and publication checks.
units.lab: Enforce a model contract with declared column types, build a compatible model, then change its output type and confirm that the run fails while the earlier relation keeps 42.

units.title: Model versions and semantic compatibility
units.outcome: Manage a semantic model change with explicit consumer versioning.
key_terms: Model version
One numbered implementation of a model declared under `versions`, with `defined_in` naming its SQL file and its own relation.
latest_version
The version an unpinned `ref` resolves to, which need not be the highest version number declared.
Versioned ref
A reference such as `ref('customer_value', version=1)` that pins a consumer to one model version.
Semantic change
A change in meaning that keeps the column name and type, such as an amount switching from gross 100 to net 80.
Migration
The planned move of each consumer from an old version to a new one before the old version is removed.
units.theory:
A model version identifies a particular contract. Consumers can reference an explicit version or follow the declared latest version. Those choices have different change behavior. An explicit version supports a controlled migration; following latest can be appropriate only when the consumer accepts the change policy.

The first case gives two versions the same column name and numeric type but different values. A stable consumer requests version 1 and receives 100, while an unversioned consumer follows version 2 and receives 80. This is intentionally a semantic change, not a parser or dtype error. A type-compatible change can still alter a model feature, dashboard metric or business decision.

The second case makes the meaning explicit: gross 100 minus returns 20 yields net 80. The dependency graph records where the calculation came from, but it does not decide whether a consumer intended gross or net. Versioning, descriptions, comparison evidence and a migration plan work together.
units.syntax: The model metadata declares latest_version and its versions, with defined_in pointing to the implementation files. ref('customer_value', version=1) selects an explicit contract. A plain ref follows the declared latest version. Inspect both the resolved database result and manifest dependency information.

worked.title: Resolve explicit and latest consumers
worked.explanation: The first project builds both versions and two consumers. Their results demonstrate the consequence of version selection while keeping the output type unchanged. The example avoids implying that a version number automatically guarantees compatibility.
worked.expected: The explicit v1 consumer returns 100; the latest v2 consumer returns 80.

worked.title: Name the semantic difference
worked.explanation: The second project computes a net quantity from its defined components and records the dependency edge. It provides enough meaning to explain why a consumer might need a different version or retraining.
worked.expected: Net is 80, derived from gross 100 and returns 20.

exercises.title: Pin a consumer
exercises.task: Change the latest consumer to request version 1 explicitly.
exercises.check: It returns 100.
exercises.hint: Use the version argument.
exercises.answer: Pinning defines the chosen contract. It also creates a responsibility to review and migrate deliberately when the old version is retired.

exercises.title: Change latest selection
exercises.task: Declare version 1 as latest in the fixture.
exercises.check: The unversioned consumer follows that declaration.
exercises.hint: Latest is project metadata.
exercises.answer: The behavior is controlled by configuration, not a universal semantic ordering. Keep release and consumer expectations explicit.

exercises.title: Add a type-compatible defect
exercises.task: Change the value while keeping the same type and name.
exercises.check: Schema checks alone can still pass.
exercises.hint: Meaning is not captured by dtype.
exercises.answer: Add semantic reconciliation and consumer-level checks. A feature can remain Float64 while changing units or time windows.

exercises.title: Design a model migration
exercises.task: Explain what a trained model needs when its input changes from gross to net.
exercises.check: The answer includes feature version and validation.
exercises.hint: The old coefficients were trained under a different meaning.
exercises.answer: Evaluate or retrain under the new feature contract, compare decisions and retain a rollback-compatible bundle. Do not change the upstream alias silently.

exercises.title: Inspect lineage
exercises.task: Find the dependency for the net model in the manifest.
exercises.check: It points to the declared base model.
exercises.hint: Lineage records a relationship.
exercises.answer: Use lineage to identify affected consumers. It does not itself prove that the calculation answers their intended question.

exercises.title: Retain rollback information
exercises.task: List the artifacts needed to restore a previous consumer contract.
exercises.check: They identify source, model version and validated data/interface.
exercises.hint: A version label alone is insufficient.
exercises.answer: Retain the implementation, dependency versions, schema/semantic definition and accepted evidence. A rollback should restore a coherent bundle.

units.diagnosis: If a result changes without a schema error, inspect semantic definitions and version resolution. An unversioned ref can follow a new latest contract intentionally. If a pinned consumer fails after removal of an old version, follow the migration policy instead of silently retargeting it.
units.transfer: Demonstrate the changed result, identify affected consumers and define validation and rollback requirements. Carry the same discipline into ML feature and model artifact versions.
units.lab: Publish two versions of a model, query a consumer pinned to version 1 and one that follows the latest version, and name the gross-to-net change that separates 100 from 80.

units.title: Selectors, graph expansion and state comparison
units.outcome: Construct and inspect a reproducible selection against an explicit baseline.
key_terms: Node selection
The `--select` syntax that limits a command to named resources, tags, paths or graph neighborhoods.
Tag
A label assigned in configuration that `--select tag:name` uses to choose a group of resources.
Graph operator
A plus sign before or after a selector that adds the selected node's ancestors or descendants.
state:modified
A selector that compares the project with a saved manifest given by `--state` and chooses the nodes whose definitions changed.
Manifest
The manifest.json artifact describing every parsed node, its configuration and its dependencies.
units.theory:
Selection controls which resources a command considers. A tag-based selection expresses a group chosen by project metadata; graph operators expand to related resources. State selection compares current project metadata with a saved manifest. These mechanisms can reduce work, but they are not themselves tests of scientific correctness or deployment safety.

The first case tags a base model and selects it with its downstream dependent. The unrelated model is excluded. The second saves a manifest, changes one source file and uses state:modified+ to include the changed model and its downstream consumer. The selected set is inspected explicitly before any claim about reduced validation is made.

A state comparison depends on the baseline manifest. Keeping that baseline inside the directory that the next command overwrites can destroy the comparison. Save it separately with its source revision and environment identity. Also distinguish a changed definition from changed underlying data: a source can receive new records while the model file remains unchanged.
units.syntax: ls returns the selected resource list without running model transformations. tag:feature+ adds downstream graph expansion. state:modified+ compares definitions against --state and includes downstream resources. The program uses --resource-type model and --output name so its expected set is explicit. Keep state artifacts outside the active target output directory.

worked.title: Select a tagged subgraph
worked.explanation: The first project has a tagged base model, its child and an unrelated model. The actual list result must contain exactly base and child. This validates selection semantics without treating the selection as an executed data test.
worked.expected: The selected model names are base and child.

worked.title: Compare against a saved manifest
worked.explanation: The second case saves a prior manifest before editing base.sql. The state selector includes the modified base and its dependent child. The baseline remains separate from the command's new target artifacts.
worked.expected: Changed and downstream selection contains both models.

exercises.title: Remove graph expansion
exercises.task: Select tag:feature without the plus suffix.

reasoning.why: tag:feature matches only base, the one model with the tag. The plus suffix adds descendants, which is why example_one returns base and child.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming that child inherits the tag because it reads from base would leave child out of a run that needs it, or include it in an audit list incorrectly.
reasoning.verify: Run dbt ls --select tag:feature --resource-type model --output name and expect only base.

exercises.check: Only the explicitly tagged model is selected.
exercises.hint: Tags and dependency traversal are different operations.
exercises.answer: Use graph operators deliberately and inspect the returned set. A tag on one model does not automatically label every downstream consumer.

exercises.title: Add an unrelated change
exercises.task: Edit the unrelated model and inspect state selection.

reasoning.why: state:modified compares the current manifest to the stored copy. Editing unrelated adds it to the modified set, while unrelated has no children to add with the plus.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming a command that ran successfully selected what was intended skips the check of the actual returned names.
reasoning.verify: Edit unrelated.sql to select 10 as x and run ls with --state previous_state --select state:modified+; expect unrelated in the list alongside any other edited models.

exercises.check: The changed node appears under the matching state selector.
exercises.hint: Compare with the saved manifest.
exercises.answer: Record the baseline revision and exact selection expression. The expected scope should be reviewed rather than inferred from a successful command.

exercises.title: Protect the baseline
exercises.task: Store prior manifest data outside target/.

reasoning.why: The reference copies target/manifest.json into previous_state before editing base. If the baseline lived in target/, the next parse would overwrite it with the new manifest.
reasoning.wrong: Pointing --state at target itself compares a manifest to itself and returns no modified nodes, which looks like nothing changed.
reasoning.verify: Run parse again after the edit, then check that previous_state/manifest.json still has base's original checksum and the state selection still returns base and child.

exercises.check: The next invocation does not overwrite it.
exercises.hint: The active output directory is mutable.
exercises.answer: Use a dedicated state directory or immutable CI artifact. A self-overwritten baseline can incorrectly make changes appear absent.

exercises.title: Change only data
exercises.task: Explain why new source rows can matter without a model-file edit.

reasoning.why: state:modified compares definitions like SQL text and config. New rows in a seed or source change the data but not the definition.
reasoning.wrong: Running only modified models after a data load would skip models that depend on the new data and leave their tables out of date.
reasoning.verify: Append a row to a seed without editing any SQL, run state:modified+, and observe that no model is selected even though downstream results would change.

exercises.check: The answer distinguishes definitions from data state.
exercises.hint: state:modified is not a data freshness check.
exercises.answer: Use the selection appropriate to the data update and validate relevant outputs. Definition comparison alone cannot establish that existing materializations are current.

exercises.title: Inspect selected tests
exercises.task: Include tests and examine the resource types returned.

reasoning.why: Dropping --resource-type model and adding a test on base lets ls return tests attached to selected models. This depends on the indirect selection mode.
reasoning.wrong: Running dbt test --select state:modified when no tests are attached returns success with zero tests, which is not a validation.
reasoning.verify: Add a not_null test on base.x, run ls --select state:modified+ without the resource filter, and expect the test node next to base and child.

exercises.check: The intended tests are visible in the selection.
exercises.hint: Selecting models is not proof of test inclusion.
exercises.answer: Review indirect-selection policy and the actual result list. An empty test selection must not be reported as a successful validation suite.

exercises.title: Record a CI decision
exercises.task: List the evidence needed to justify a reduced build.

reasoning.why: A reduced build is justified only when the baseline, selection expression, selected nodes and actual outcomes are all recorded together.
reasoning.wrong: Recording only that CI passed hides which models were skipped and why.
reasoning.verify: Store the baseline manifest hash, the exact command, the ls output and run_results statuses, and check that a reviewer can rebuild the same list.

exercises.check: It includes baseline, selection, dependencies and executed results.
exercises.hint: A selection plan is only one stage.
exercises.answer: Keep the source revision, manifest identity, selected node set, commands and actual outcomes. Use a broader gate when the change affects shared semantics or operational assumptions.

units.diagnosis: Unexpectedly small selections can result from tags, graph direction, indirect-test rules or an overwritten baseline. Inspect ls output before executing a destructive or expensive command. A successful selector command with zero intended resources is not a completed validation.
units.transfer: Explain which dependencies and tests are included and which data changes are outside the comparison. The later CI lessons connect that selection to real execution and deferral.
units.lab: List the models selected by tag:feature+, then save a manifest, change one model and select state:modified+ against that saved baseline.

units.title: Documentation, catalogs, exposures and ownership
units.outcome: Build documentation that joins observed structure with authored meaning and ownership.
key_terms: catalog.json
The artifact written by `dbt docs generate` that records the columns and types actually found in the database.
Description
Human-written meaning for a model or column in YAML, stored in the manifest and shown in generated documentation.
Exposure
A YAML declaration of a downstream consumer such as a dashboard, with its type, owner and `depends_on` references.
Lineage
The dependency path from sources through models to exposures, read from the manifest graph.
Owner
The person or team an exposure names as accountable for a consumer, so a breaking change has someone to notify.
units.theory:
Documentation has both structural and semantic parts. A database catalog can identify a column's physical type, while a project description explains what the value means. Neither substitutes for the other. A field named total needs a grain, unit, time window and inclusion policy before a consumer can interpret it reliably.

The first case generates real dbt documentation artifacts after building a mart. The catalog records the observed database column, and the manifest records a declared exposure depending on that mart. An exposure represents a downstream use such as a dashboard or application. It improves lineage and ownership visibility, but it does not prove that an external consumer is currently healthy or actually using the declared version.

The second case demonstrates a structurally documented but semantically undescribed model. Its integer type is available, yet its description is empty. A documentation build can therefore succeed while important meaning remains absent. Treat generated artifacts as a foundation for review, not an automatic substitute for authored definitions.
units.syntax: docs generate inspects the built project and writes catalog.json alongside manifest.json. Model and column descriptions live in schema metadata. An exposure names its type, owner and ref-based dependencies. The classroom inspects these JSON artifacts locally; it does not start a separate docs web server or claim that arbitrary generated HTML is a trusted worker result.

worked.title: Connect physical and declared information
worked.explanation: The first case checks a total column in the catalog and the exposure's dependency in the manifest. It combines observed database structure with declared project meaning without confusing the two.
worked.expected: The catalog contains total and the decision-report exposure depends on mart.

worked.title: Detect missing semantics
worked.explanation: The second project builds and documents a model with no authored description. The program verifies that its physical INTEGER type is known while its description is empty.
worked.expected: The type is available, but the business description is missing.

exercises.title: Write a complete definition
exercises.task: Describe total with its grain, units and inclusion rule.

reasoning.why: mart sums amount across all orders, so its grain is one row for the whole table. With the seed rows 5 and 7, total is 12 in the same unit as amount.
reasoning.wrong: Writing total as the total amount repeats the column name without saying what is included.
reasoning.verify: Write the description, then ask whether a reader could predict 12 from the two seed rows without reading the SQL.

exercises.check: A reader can interpret the quantity without guessing.
exercises.hint: A column name alone is insufficient.
exercises.answer: State which records contribute, the grouping key, time boundary and unit. Keep the definition aligned with the model and tests.

exercises.title: Add a downstream consumer
exercises.task: Declare a second exposure with its owner and dependency.

reasoning.why: An exposure declares a consumer and its dependency. dbt places it in the manifest graph so you can see who reads mart.
reasoning.wrong: Treating the exposure as proof that the dashboard exists or reads mart today is wrong, since dbt never contacts it.
reasoning.verify: Add a second exposure with depends_on ref('mart') and an owner, run docs generate, and confirm its depends_on.nodes lists model.classroom.mart.

exercises.check: The new edge appears in the manifest.
exercises.hint: Use ref-based lineage.
exercises.answer: The exposure is a maintained declaration. Validate actual consumer behavior separately and update ownership when responsibility changes.

exercises.title: Inspect physical type
exercises.task: Read the catalog's type for a column.

reasoning.why: catalog.json is built by querying the database, so it shows the real type that DuckDB stored, such as INTEGER for answer in example_two.
reasoning.wrong: Reading a catalog generated before the latest build would report an older type for a changed column.
reasoning.verify: Run build then docs generate and check catalog nodes for the column; the type should match the cast in the SQL.

exercises.check: It matches the built database representation.
exercises.hint: Compilation alone does not create the catalog observation.
exercises.answer: Generate docs against the intended materialized state and retain its invocation/source context. A stale catalog can describe an older deployment.

exercises.title: Find an undocumented field
exercises.task: Create a model column without a description.

reasoning.why: example_two has an empty description for answer. The gap remains visible in the manifest, which is the point of the exercise.
reasoning.wrong: Filling every empty description with a placeholder sentence makes the docs look complete while saying nothing.
reasoning.verify: Check that `nodes['model.classroom.answer']['description'] == ''` in the manifest and that its `columns` map is empty, because example_two has no schema.yml; the gap stays until someone writes a real description.

exercises.check: The documentation gap remains visible.
exercises.hint: Success of docs generate is not prose completeness.
exercises.answer: Add a semantic review gate appropriate to the project. Avoid automatically filling descriptions with generic repeated text.

exercises.title: Separate lineage from execution
exercises.task: Explain what an exposure cannot establish.

reasoning.why: An exposure records a declared dependency only. It does not show that the dashboard ran, loaded, or displayed the current total.
reasoning.wrong: Citing the exposure as evidence the report refreshed confuses declared lineage with observed execution.
reasoning.verify: Compare the exposure with an actual dashboard refresh log; only the log shows a run.

exercises.check: It cannot prove the external dashboard ran successfully.
exercises.hint: Declared relationships differ from runtime observations.
exercises.answer: Combine lineage with actual deployment and service evidence when making operational claims. Keep those evidence sources separately identifiable.

exercises.title: Export a compact review record
exercises.task: Select useful metadata from the generated artifacts.

reasoning.why: A short review record picks the description, owner, exposure dependency and artifact identifiers from manifest.json and catalog.json.
reasoning.wrong: Copying the full artifacts into the record makes review hard and duplicates files that change with every run.
reasoning.verify: Write a small JSON record with the model description, exposure owner, dependency nodes and a hash of each artifact, then check each value against the source files.

exercises.check: The record contains meaning, ownership and dependency identifiers.
exercises.hint: Do not dump an entire large manifest into a user message.
exercises.answer: Keep a bounded summary with links or hashes identifying the underlying artifacts. The full files remain the detailed evidence in a durable project.

units.diagnosis: A missing catalog node may mean the model was not materialized or the wrong environment was inspected. An empty description is an authored-content gap. An exposure pointing to the wrong model is a lineage defect even if the database query succeeds. Diagnose these separately.
units.transfer: Review a consumer's dependency and record which claims are declarations versus runtime evidence. This creates a useful handoff for analysts, data scientists and operators.
units.lab: Generate documentation for a described mart with an exposure, read the catalog and manifest, and detect a model whose type is known but whose description is missing.

units.title: Publication gates after materialization
units.outcome: Separate candidate computation from accepted publication.
key_terms: Candidate relation
A relation built by the current run that consumers must not rely on until its checks pass.
Publication gate
The rule that writes the accepted output only when the invocation succeeds and every relevant run_results status passes.
Accepted artifact
The consumer-facing output that passed the gate; a failed candidate leaves it unchanged.
Publication receipt
A record of the data, schema, source version and checks that justified accepting an artifact.
units.theory:
Materialization and publication are different actions. A model relation may exist even when later tests fail. If consumers must not see invalid data, they need an accepted-output boundary that is updated only after the required evidence passes. A successful SQL statement is insufficient for that decision.

The example builds a candidate relation with key tests and publishes a small JSON output only when the complete invocation and relevant statuses pass. The bad fixture still materializes two rows, but no published file is created. The program checks both facts so it cannot confuse detection with transactional rollback.

This is a local publication gate, not a distributed transaction across a warehouse and an object store. A real deployment needs atomic pointer or version selection, ownership, retry behavior and recovery after uncertain outcomes. The lesson establishes the decision rule and evidence boundary that those mechanisms must implement.
units.syntax: Check result.success and the relevant run_results statuses before writing the accepted output. Keep the candidate relation separate from the consumer-facing artifact. A publication receipt should identify the data, schema, source version and checks that justified acceptance. A stale successful artifact must not qualify a new candidate.

worked.title: Publish an accepted candidate
worked.explanation: The valid two-row fixture passes both key conditions and produces a JSON artifact. The program confirms that the artifact exists only after successful evidence is available.
worked.expected: Two candidate rows are present and publication is true.

worked.title: Keep a failed candidate out of the accepted boundary
worked.explanation: The duplicate-key fixture causes a failed test. The database relation still exists, but the publication step is skipped. This is the intended failure policy, not a missing output bug.
worked.expected: Two candidate rows exist, but publication is false.

exercises.title: Change the failure condition
exercises.task: Add a domain test that rejects negative amounts.

reasoning.why: In this lesson ready is materialized from events before tests run. An accepted_range test with min_value 0 on value makes a negative row a meaningful failure that blocks publication.
reasoning.wrong: Treating any warning as a block mixes noise with real failures and trains people to ignore the gate.
reasoning.verify: Seed a row with value -3, run build, and confirm the range test fails and published.json is not written.

exercises.check: The candidate can be blocked by a meaningful semantic failure.
exercises.hint: Key validity is only one dimension.
exercises.answer: Define the condition and verify a designed negative fixture. Do not treat every possible warning as equivalent to an accepted result.

exercises.title: Inspect candidate state
exercises.task: Query the bad relation after failure.

reasoning.why: After the duplicate-id build fails, the ready table still holds 2 rows. The reference asserts this count in both cases.
reasoning.wrong: Assuming a failed build removes the table hides that its bad rows are still readable.
reasoning.verify: Query select count(*) from ready after the failure and expect 2.

exercises.check: Its materialized rows are still observable.
exercises.hint: Tests may occur after model creation.
exercises.answer: Use this observation to design consumer isolation. Hiding an error message does not remove invalid data from a relation.

exercises.title: Retain an accepted version
exercises.task: Keep a prior valid artifact while a new candidate fails.

reasoning.why: Consumers should read a named accepted version, not the newest file. The failed candidate must not replace the prior accepted output.
reasoning.wrong: Overwriting published.json before tests finish would replace good data with a candidate that later fails.
reasoning.verify: Publish the good case, then run the bad case and confirm the earlier published.json is still present and unchanged.

exercises.check: The accepted version remains identifiable.
exercises.hint: Separate candidate and accepted paths.
exercises.answer: A consumer should follow a declared accepted version or pointer, not whichever file was most recently written.

exercises.title: Handle an uncertain write
exercises.task: Describe a publication timeout after the write may have occurred.

reasoning.why: A timeout after writing leaves it unknown whether the file exists. Checking its identifier or hash resolves this before retrying.
reasoning.wrong: Retrying blindly can publish twice in a system where writes are not idempotent.
reasoning.verify: Compute the expected hash, check the destination for that hash, and retry only if it is missing.

exercises.check: The response reconciles identity before retrying.
exercises.hint: An unknown outcome is not a confirmed failure.
exercises.answer: Read the intended publication identifier or hash and determine whether it exists. Blind retries can duplicate side effects in less idempotent systems.

exercises.title: Record the evidence
exercises.task: Add a compact receipt beside the accepted data.

reasoning.why: A receipt beside the data records input version, model version, test outcomes and output hash.
reasoning.wrong: Recording only a timestamp says nothing about which data or checks were accepted.
reasoning.verify: Write the receipt, then confirm each field matches run_results.json and the published file's hash.

exercises.check: It identifies source, checks and data identity.
exercises.hint: A file timestamp is not enough.
exercises.answer: Retain input and model versions, schema/grain, executed test outcomes and output identity. Keep provenance and semantic quality as distinct claims.

exercises.title: Test a stale artifact
exercises.task: Change source data but reuse an old successful run_results file.

reasoning.why: A stale run_results.json describes an earlier invocation. Reusing it after changing the source would accept data that was never tested.
reasoning.wrong: Checking only that statuses say pass, without matching the invocation id, lets old evidence approve new data.
reasoning.verify: Change the seed, keep the old run_results, and confirm a gate that compares invocation ids rejects publication.

exercises.check: A reviewed gate rejects the mismatched evidence.
exercises.hint: Bind evidence to the current candidate.
exercises.answer: Use invocation and source/data identities. A successful result from a different run cannot justify publication of changed data.

units.diagnosis: If invalid data appears despite a failed build, inspect the consumer-facing boundary. If publication is missing after success, check the exact selected statuses and artifact path. Keep failures visible and reconcile uncertain outcomes before retrying. A gate that simply ignores failed tests is not recovery.
units.transfer: Demonstrate both paths and retain a source-bound decision record. Extend the mechanism to an atomic version pointer and a tested recovery plan in a durable owned environment.
units.lab: Build a candidate relation and record publication only when every test passes, then show that a failed uniqueness test leaves the candidate built but unpublished.
references: dbt reference: Run results JSON file

units.title: Metric contracts and valid denominators
units.outcome: Publish a metric with a complete numerator/denominator contract and an independent check.
key_terms: Metric contract
A declaration of a metric's numerator, denominator, grain and edge-case policy so every consumer computes it the same way.
Grain
The entity and time level at which one metric row is defined, such as one region per day.
Pooled rate
Total numerator divided by total denominator, which weights each group by its denominator.
Average of rates
The unweighted mean of group rates, which gives a small group the same weight as a large one and usually differs from the pooled rate.
Zero-denominator policy
The declared result, such as null, for a group whose denominator is zero.
units.theory:
A metric is a defined quantity, not merely a SQL expression. Its contract names the population, unit of analysis, numerator, denominator, time window and treatment of missing or invalid records. Two expressions can both execute and still answer different questions. The first responsibility is to define the desired quantity.

The worked fixture pools successes and trials by cohort. Cohort A contains rows with very different trial counts, so averaging row-level rates gives a misleading result for the pooled-trial question. This is the same statistical issue seen in the Polars path, now expressed in a tested warehouse model. The transfer matters because a semantic error can survive changes in language or tooling.

The examples use ordinary dbt models and SQL. They do not claim to run a hosted semantic layer or MetricFlow service. A future semantic-layer integration should preserve these contracts and test its actual query semantics. Installing another tool would not decide the correct denominator.
units.syntax: Aggregate numerator and denominator separately, then divide with a declared zero-denominator policy. Keep the denominator in the output for review and uncertainty calculations. A GROUP BY changes result grain, so identify its keys explicitly. Avoid using an unweighted AVG of precomputed rates unless equal-row weighting is the intended estimand.

worked.title: Compute cohort-level pooled rates
worked.explanation: The valid model retains trial counts beside rates. The program checks exact cohort values in the actual DuckDB relation. This makes both the weighting and the evidence amount visible.
worked.expected: Cohort A is 0.1 from 100 trials; cohort B is 0.5 from 2 trials.

worked.title: Execute a mathematically different metric
worked.explanation: The second model averages two row rates and returns about 0.545 rather than 0.1. The SQL is valid; the defect is the mismatch between its weighting and the pooled-trial question.
worked.expected: Equal-row averaging differs by more than 0.4 from the pooled rate.

exercises.title: Write the population
exercises.task: Specify which trial records belong in the metric.
exercises.check: The inclusion and time rules are explicit.
exercises.hint: A WHERE clause should implement a definition.
exercises.answer: State eligibility, time, treatment of missingness and duplicate policy before writing the SQL. Keep those rules with the metric owner.

exercises.title: Pool across cohorts
exercises.task: Compute the all-trial rate.
exercises.check: The rate is 11/102.
exercises.hint: Use count weighting.
exercises.answer: A mean of cohort rates would give equal cohort weight and a different target. Choose the weighting unit from the question.
exercises.answer_code:
# Uses the tempfile import and the project(), invoke() and rows() helpers in main.py.
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    p = project(
        d,
        models={
            "overall": (
                "select sum(successes)::double / nullif(sum(trials), 0) as rate, "
                "sum(trials) as denominator from {{ ref('counts') }}"
            )
        },
        seeds={"counts": "cohort,successes,trials\nA,1,1\nA,9,99\nB,1,2\n"},
    )
    invoke(p, "build")
    assert rows(p, "select rate, denominator from overall") == [(11 / 102, 102)]

exercises.title: Test empty evidence
exercises.task: Add a zero-trial cohort.
exercises.check: Its rate follows an explicit undefined-value policy.
exercises.hint: No trials do not prove zero success probability.
exercises.answer: Return null or a separate no-evidence status and retain the denominator. Do not silently manufacture observed failures.

exercises.title: Preserve counts
exercises.task: Show numerator and denominator with every rate.
exercises.check: The estimate can be independently reconstructed.
exercises.hint: A percentage loses sample-size information.
exercises.answer: Counts support intervals and comparison of evidence. Preserve the original metric grain while joining other descriptive fields.

exercises.title: Prevent join inflation
exercises.task: Add a duplicate descriptive dimension and test reconciliation.
exercises.check: The gate detects changed totals or cardinality.
exercises.hint: A valid metric can be corrupted by enrichment.
exercises.answer: Validate the relationship and compare numerator/denominator totals before and after joins. Distinct on a final display is not a general repair.

exercises.title: Review semantic-layer claims
exercises.task: Explain what extra qualification a metric service would need.
exercises.check: It includes actual generated queries and equivalent outputs.
exercises.hint: A declaration is not execution.
exercises.answer: Use known fixtures and compare service results with an independent oracle, including nulls, joins, time boundaries and filters. Keep platform setup explicit.

units.diagnosis: A large rate change may come from a changed denominator rather than a changed phenomenon. Inspect grouping, source coverage and join multiplicities. A query that compiles and passes key tests can still implement the wrong estimand. Make the metric definition and independent fixture arithmetic part of review.
units.transfer: Carry it across SQL, Polars and downstream model dashboards without changing its meaning. Treat semantic-layer adoption as an additional implementation to qualify against that contract.
units.lab: Compute pooled cohort rates in SQL from success and trial counts, check them against independent arithmetic, and compare an equal-row average that differs by more than 0.4.

units.title: Temporal data products and late-known facts
units.outcome: Produce a historical feature relation with explicit entity, time and version semantics.
key_terms: Event time
When something happened in the world, stored here as event_at.
Availability time
When a fact became known to the system, stored here as known_at; a prediction cannot use the fact before this time.
Point-in-time join
A join that keeps only facts whose event time and availability time are both at or before the prediction cutoff.
Feature leakage
Using information that was not available at prediction time, which makes measured accuracy look better than deployment can achieve.
row_number selection
Ranking rows with `row_number()` to keep the latest known version; eligibility must be filtered before ranking, not after.
units.theory:
Historical correctness depends on what was knowable at the decision time. An event can occur before a cutoff but arrive after it. A correction can revise an old event using information discovered later. Selecting only event_time<=cutoff can therefore expose future knowledge to a historical analysis or model.

The example represents both event_at and known_at. It joins requests to eligible feature records and uses row_number to select the latest version after applying both clocks. The counterexample omits the availability condition and returns a strikingly different value for the first request. The program compares the actual model relations, not only the SQL strings.

This small candidate join is designed for inspection, not arbitrary scale. A large implementation needs an appropriate physical strategy, snapshots or source history while preserving the same semantics. The schema must also distinguish unavailable information from a legitimate zero, and requests with no eligible history must remain accounted for.
units.syntax: The join combines entity identity with event and availability cutoffs. row_number partitions by request identity and orders eligible versions by the declared version keys. Eligibility must be applied before selecting the latest row. The fixture uses integer time keys for transparent arithmetic; a real contract must define timezone and boundary semantics for timestamps.

worked.title: Select only known information
worked.explanation: At request cutoff 5, the event at 4 is not known until 7, so the correct result uses the earlier value 10. At cutoff 9, value 30 is eligible. The ordering chooses among already eligible records.
worked.expected: The available feature values are [10, 30].

worked.title: Observe a leaking historical model
worked.explanation: The second case omits the known_at condition. It selects 999 for the first request, even though that information was unavailable at cutoff 5. Both models execute successfully, making the semantic failure visible.
worked.expected: The event-only model returns [999, 30].

exercises.title: Add an unmatched request
exercises.task: Create a cutoff before any eligible feature.
exercises.check: The request is explicitly retained or counted as unmatched.
exercises.hint: The example inner join has a coverage limit.
exercises.answer: Left-join selected results back to the request population and report missing-feature reasons. Do not drop difficult requests before evaluating a model.

exercises.title: Change the availability clock
exercises.task: Make the revised event known at 4.
exercises.check: It is eligible for cutoff 5.
exercises.hint: The two-clock rule remains unchanged.
exercises.answer: The result changes because the source history changed. Preserve that history/version when reporting a retrospective analysis.
exercises.answer_code:
# Uses the tempfile import and the project(), invoke() and rows() helpers in main.py.
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    sql = (
        "select request_id, value from (select r.request_id, f.value, "
        "row_number() over (partition by r.request_id order by f.event_at desc, "
        "f.known_at desc) as rank from {{ ref('requests') }} r join "
        "{{ ref('features') }} f on r.customer = f.customer "
        "and f.event_at <= r.cutoff and f.known_at <= r.cutoff) where rank = 1"
    )
    p = project(
        d,
        models={"training_features": sql},
        seeds={
            "requests": "request_id,customer,cutoff\n1,10,5\n2,10,9\n",
            "features": "customer,event_at,known_at,value\n10,2,3,10\n10,4,4,999\n10,8,8,30\n",
        },
    )
    invoke(p, "build")
    result = rows(p, "select request_id, value from training_features order by request_id")
    assert result == [(1, 999), (2, 30)]

exercises.title: Test equal cutoffs
exercises.task: Place an event exactly on the request boundary.
exercises.check: Its treatment matches the documented inclusive rule.
exercises.hint: Boundary operators are assumptions.
exercises.answer: The example uses <=. Some systems require a transaction or ingestion watermark that changes what equality means operationally.

exercises.title: Add version ties
exercises.task: Create two eligible versions with equal event and known keys.
exercises.check: A further deterministic authority rule or rejection is required.
exercises.hint: row_number needs a meaningful total ordering.
exercises.answer: Do not rely on accidental database ordering. Define an additional version identifier or fail ambiguous input.

exercises.title: Compare with a snapshot
exercises.task: Explain why a periodic snapshot may not capture every intermediate state.
exercises.check: The answer distinguishes observed state from complete source history.
exercises.hint: A snapshot sees what was present when it ran.
exercises.answer: Choose a source history mechanism that supports the desired retrospective question. Do not reinterpret snapshot observation time as business-effective time.

exercises.title: Validate with an oracle
exercises.task: Recompute the two request values in Python from the tiny rows.
exercises.check: The oracle returns 10 and 30.
exercises.hint: Use the explicit eligibility inequalities.
exercises.answer: Keep this independent fixture in regression tests. SQL execution success alone cannot identify a temporal leakage error.

units.diagnosis: If a historical score is suspiciously good, inspect availability and label timing before interpreting model quality. If rows disappear, reconcile request coverage. If results vary on rerun, inspect version ties and ordering. Fix the temporal data contract before adjusting the model.
units.transfer: Demonstrate a late-known counterexample and retain request coverage. This prepares the feature-store and ML engineering route to test actual retrieval against a meaningful temporal oracle.
units.lab: Build a point-in-time feature model that requires event and known times to precede each request cutoff, and compare it with an event-time-only model that returns 999.

units.title: Local packages and reusable project dependencies
units.outcome: Prepare and inspect a real reusable dbt dependency with an explicit source boundary.
key_terms: dbt package
A dbt project whose macros and models another project installs and uses.
packages.yml
The file listing package dependencies; here it points to a local path, so installation needs no download.
dbt deps
The command that installs declared packages and writes package-lock.yml; it must run before a build that uses them.
Package namespace
The prefix that calls a package macro by package name, such as `classroom_utils.add_one`, avoiding name collisions.
package-lock.yml
The file that pins resolved package versions for repeatable installs; it records what was installed, not that the code is trustworthy.
units.theory:
A dbt package is another project that contributes resources such as macros or models. Declaring a package and preparing it are separate steps. A model can reference a package namespace only after the dependency is available under the project's configured package installation location. This is a project dependency boundary, not a reason to download arbitrary code during a learner run.

The example uses a local package created inside the owned temporary project. Its macro adds one to a supplied SQL expression. The deps command prepares that local dependency and writes a lock artifact; the subsequent build resolves the namespace and executes the emitted SQL in DuckDB. No registry or network request is needed.

A package name or lockfile is not a trust certificate. Review source, license, versions and transitive requirements before adopting an external package. A local path dependency can change without an external release number, so a reproducible project also needs its source identity. Keep authored local packages separate from generated installation directories and never treat copied build output as the maintained source.
units.syntax: packages.yml declares a local package path. The package has its own dbt_project.yml, name and macros directory. A namespace-qualified call such as classroom_utils.add_one identifies the package that supplies the macro. Run deps before compile/build, then inspect package-lock.yml and the manifest macro entry. Local dependencies are the only package preparation performed in these offline examples.

worked.title: Use a prepared local package
worked.explanation: The first case writes a real local package and prepares it with dbt deps. Its macro appears in the manifest, the lock artifact exists, and the resulting model returns 42. Each observation comes from the actual toolchain.
worked.expected: The macro is registered, the lockfile is written and the model returns 42.

worked.title: Diagnose missing preparation
worked.explanation: The second project attempts compilation before deps and expects rejection. Preparing the existing local package is then sufficient for compilation to succeed. The model logic itself has not changed.
worked.expected: Missing dependency preparation fails; local deps followed by compile succeeds.

exercises.title: Inspect package identity
exercises.task: Find the package name and macro namespace.
exercises.check: They identify classroom_utils and add_one.
exercises.hint: Project names determine namespaces.
exercises.answer: Keep names stable and avoid accidental collisions. A namespace is a source-resolution mechanism, not a guarantee that the macro is trustworthy.

exercises.title: Change package logic
exercises.task: Change the local macro to add 2 and rebuild.
exercises.check: The output becomes 43.
exercises.hint: The dependency source changed.
exercises.answer: Record the source change and affected consumers. A local path can change even when no remote version declaration changes.
exercises.answer_code:
# Uses the tempfile import and the package_project(), invoke() and rows() helpers in main.py.
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    p = package_project(d)
    (p / "local_packages/classroom_utils/macros/add_one.sql").write_text(
        "{% macro add_one(value) %} (({{ value }}) + 2) {% endmacro %}"
    )
    invoke(p, "deps")
    invoke(p, "build")
    assert rows(p, "select answer from answer") == [(43,)]

exercises.title: Read the lock artifact
exercises.task: Inspect package-lock.yml after deps.
exercises.check: The prepared dependency is recorded.
exercises.hint: A lock supports reproducibility only for its declared semantics.
exercises.answer: Retain the package declaration and corresponding source. Review what is pinned versus what remains a mutable local path.

exercises.title: Keep generated paths separate
exercises.task: Identify the authored local package and installed package directory.
exercises.check: Their maintenance roles differ.
exercises.hint: Do not edit a generated copy as the source.
exercises.answer: Update the maintained package, rerun preparation and validate consumers. Generated installation trees should not enter the portable source payload as accidental build output.

exercises.title: Review an external package
exercises.task: List evidence needed before adding a registry dependency.
exercises.check: It includes source, version, license and required capabilities.
exercises.hint: A package can execute templating logic during compilation.
exercises.answer: Use a reviewed dependency policy and prepare downloads explicitly. Opening a lesson must not silently obtain or execute a new package.

exercises.title: Test namespace failure
exercises.task: Use an incorrect package namespace and observe compilation.
exercises.check: The undefined macro is rejected.
exercises.hint: Check discovery before changing SQL arithmetic.
exercises.answer: The diagnostic concerns dependency/name resolution. Preserve it and correct the declaration or call rather than inventing a fallback calculation.

units.diagnosis: An undefined package macro can result from missing preparation, a wrong package name or an unavailable resource. Check the dependency declaration, installed paths and manifest before modifying the consumer's SQL. Do not solve a local preparation problem by enabling unrelated network access inside the classroom.
units.transfer: Demonstrate its missing-dependency failure and a reviewed source change. Extend the same discipline to external packages only in a deliberately prepared project with suitable version and trust controls.
units.lab: Prepare a local package with dbt deps, use its add_one macro in a model that returns 42, and show that compiling before the package is prepared fails.

units.title: Targets, environments and owned database routing
units.outcome: Run a project against an explicitly identified owned target and verify its actual destination.
key_terms: Target
A named output under a profile that sets the database, schema and settings for one environment.
--target
The command option that selects which output of the profile a run uses.
target.name
The Jinja variable holding the active target's name, which models and macros can read or return as data.
Schema routing
Building each target's relations in its own schema; two schemas in one DuckDB file separate names, not access or failures.
units.theory:
A target selects a named execution environment from a profile. A project can use the same model definitions while changing database or schema routing and other adapter settings. That flexibility must not turn into ambient selection of a valuable database. Every example here uses one newly created local DuckDB file; dev and prod are synthetic schema labels inside it.

The first case builds the same model into separate schemas and returns target.name as data so the routing is visible. The result demonstrates environment selection without implying that two schemas in one file provide the isolation, access control or durability of independent production systems.

units.title: Deferral and the choice of upstream state
units.outcome: Use deferral with an explicit upstream-state contract.
key_terms: Deferral
Running with `--defer --state` so a `ref` to an unselected node can resolve to the relation recorded in a saved manifest.
State manifest
A manifest.json from an accepted baseline run, saved outside target/ so later runs cannot overwrite it.
--favor-state
An option that makes deferral prefer the state relation even when a relation for the node already exists in the current target.
dbt clone
A command (dbt 1.6 and later) that creates selected nodes in the current target from state relations, as a view on DuckDB, which has no zero-copy clone.
units.theory:
Deferral lets a selected model resolve unselected dependencies using a prior manifest's relation information. It can support a small development or CI build that reuses accepted upstream relations. The manifest is therefore more than a source checksum: it identifies concrete relations that must exist and be appropriate for the intended test.

The first case builds a baseline in the synthetic prod schema, saves its manifest, and builds only a child in dev. No dev parent is created, so the child resolves the accepted prod parent. The second case gives dev its own parent with a different value. Normal deferral and favor-state then produce different observed results.

This difference matters when developers assume defer always means use production data. Existing target relations can influence resolution unless the selection policy explicitly favors the saved state. A reliable CI recipe should state which data is being read, how that baseline is qualified and whether target relations may already exist. The local schemas are owned fixtures, not access to a real production warehouse.

`dbt clone` (dbt 1.6 and later) is the alternative when a later step needs real objects rather than compile-time references. It reads the same saved state and creates each selected node in the current target: a zero-copy clone on platforms that support one (Snowflake, Databricks and BigQuery) and otherwise a view that selects from the state's relation. It does not replace relations that already exist in the target unless `--full-refresh` is given. Deferral is usually cheaper because it creates nothing; clone is useful when a tool outside dbt, such as a dashboard, must query the development schema. Neither command checks that the baseline data is still accepted. This lesson's program uses deferral only.

units.syntax:
--defer and --state point compilation to a saved manifest for eligible unselected dependencies. --favor-state changes the preference when an existing target relation could otherwise be used. The example saves its baseline outside target/ and checks compiled SQL as well as actual result values. Qualified names in compiled SQL identify the chosen parent.

The equivalent clone step, shown for reading and not run here, would be:

```bash
dbt clone --select child --state prod_state --target dev
```

DuckDB has no zero-copy clone, so with the pinned dbt-duckdb 1.11.1 this command creates `dev.child` as a view defined as `SELECT * FROM prod.child`. Running it again reports that the relation already exists and leaves it in place.
